Myrcia almasensis - NicLugh.
PLANTAE - TRACHEOPHYTA - MAGNOLIOPSIDA - MYRTALES - MYRTACEAE - Myrcia - almasensis

Common Names: No Common Names
Synonyms: No Synonyms
Date of Assessment: 2021-02-03
Assessor(s): Rotton, H., Lima, D. & Lucas, E.
Reviewer(s): Amorim, E. & Fernandez, E.
Facilitators/Compilers: Plummer, J.
Institution(s): Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, IUCN SSC Brazil Plant Red List Authority & Centro Nacional de Conservação da Flora (CNCFlora)
Regions: Global

This species is endemic to Bahia in Brazil. Its extent of occurrence (EOO) has been estimated as 433 km2 and its area of occupancy (AOO) as 12 km2, both falling below the respective thresholds for the Endangered category. Its habitat is in continuing decline, mainly due to deforestation and clearance for urban expansion. It does occur in close proximity to a protected area but this is experiencing sporadic fire outbreaks, both man-made and natural, and has a low level of protection. The species is therefore assessed as Endangered with a restricted distribution, three known locations and a continuing decline in extent and quality of habitat.
This species is endemic to Brazil, known to occur in the state of Bahia at altitudes between 1,000 and 1,500 m asl (Nic Lughadha 1994).

There are three known localities for this species based on current literature and herbarium specimens and all have different ongoing threats in the surrounding areas, with habitat loss representing the major driver of threat.

blocks.text: Biogeographic Realm: Neotropical

The overall population size and trend of this species are unknown due to lack of available information. This species is known from four specimens collected between 1988 and 2011 and it has been described as rare (Mori et al. #12390).
Current Population Trend: Unknown

This shrub or small tree, reaching up to 5 m in height, occurs in campo rupestre or sandy grassland, often among rocky outcrops (Nic Lughadha 1994). It has been collected from the Brazilian Atlantic dry forests and the Caatinga ecoregions (Dinerstein et al. 2017).

rows: Continuing decline in area, extent and/or quality of habitat?
Inferred from ongoing threats identified within the species range, including urban and tourism expansion, fire outbreaks, and mining activities.

blocks.text: System: Terrestrial
Wild relative of a crop? No
Species not utilized: true
This species is not known to be utilised.

There are no documented current major threats to this species, however, it is present in areas which have historically been subject to high levels of deforestation and habitat loss. It has been estimated that only 50% of the Caatinga natural vegetation cover still remains (Antongiovanni et al. 2018), while only 11.4% to 16% of the original Atlantic Forest vegetation remains and c. 42% of the total forest area is represented by fragments smaller than 250 ha (Ribeiro et al. 2009). Although the deforestation rate has been decreasing in the last few years, it is still ongoing, and in the state of Bahia, only 11.1% of Atlantic Forest remains and has been continuously deforested for at least the last 30 years (Fundação SOS Mata Atlântica and INPE 2020). Mining activities, urban expansion, and tourism are major threats in the Campos Rupestre (Fernandes et al. 2020) and burning vegetation for cattle farming is common practice in this biome (Kolbek and Alves 2008, Silveira et al. 2016). Although this species may feasibly occur inside Área De Proteção Ambiental Serra Do Barbado, this protected area is threatened by sporadic fire outbreaks and has a particularly low category of protection and high rates of tourism (Romero and Woodgyer 2018).

blocks.text: There are no conservation measures in place specific for this species. It does not occur within any protected areas, but the known collection localities are in close proximity to Área De Proteção Ambiental Serra Do Barbado (UNEP-WCMC and IUCN 2021), which has suitable habitat. There are currently no ex situ collections (BGCI 2021).
